name: Remitly Global, Inc.

profile.description: Remitly Global provides digital financial services for immigrants and their families, chiefly mobile-first international money transfers to nearly 150 countries. Founded in 2011 and headquartered in Seattle, the company generated $1.64B of revenue in FY2025 and $495M in Q2 2026 (+20% YoY on +27% send volume). Co-founder Matt Oppenheimer handed the CEO role to former Amazon executive Sebastian Gunningham and moved to board chair. Q3 2026 results are scheduled for November 4, 2026, with guidance of $505-507M revenue (+20-21%) [1][6][8].

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Remitly scaled revenue from $257M in FY2020 to $1.64B in FY2025 and crossed into GAAP profitability ($67.9M net income in FY2025 after losses of $118M in FY2023), while extending into higher-value senders that drove a fourth straight guidance raise to $1.978-1.988B for FY2026 [3][6]. AI Deployment (1/2): CEO Gunningham says AI is making Remitly faster at building products and supporting customers, and the company has committed to using AI to improve customer experience, but no quantified savings or AI revenue have been disclosed [9]. Market Share (1/2): Send volume grew 27% YoY in Q2 2026, outpacing legacy rivals, but no category share data was found and revenue growth (20%) lagging volume raises take-rate questions [1][7]. Pipeline (1/2): Expansion toward broader immigrant financial services and high-value corridors is discussed, but without named launches and revenue targets [6]. R&D Intensity (1/1): FY2025 R&D of $313.9M equals 19.2% of revenue, top-quartile for payments companies [3].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): Remitly's purpose of transforming the lives of immigrants and their families with trusted financial services is specific and rooted in the founder's story of watching remittance friction while working in Kenya, a journey from a mall booth to a multi-billion-dollar fintech [12][14]. Community Impact (1/2): The company participates in Pledge 1% with giving directed at financial inclusion for immigrants, a real but modest program with no large dollar commitments disclosed [12]. Employee Retention (0/2): No turnover or tenure data was found; the founder-CEO's transition to chair marks a leadership change [8]. Insider Buying (0/2): FMP data shows zero open-market insider purchases in 2025-2026 against dozens of sales, including about 1.68M shares disposed in Q3 2026 alone [5].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically (Growth sleeve): D/E of 3.4% (1.00), ROE of 33.0% (1.00, 2x), YoY revenue growth of 20.2% in Q2 2026 (1.00), 5-year revenue CAGR of 44.8% from FY2020-FY2025 (1.00, 2x), forward P/E of 22.6 (0.94), net margin of 16.9% (0.84) and forward PEG of 0.15 per FMP (1.00, 2x). Weighted sum is 9.78/10, which rounds to 10 [3][4]. Caveat: TTM net margin and ROE are inflated by a $141M income tax benefit in Q2 2026 (a valuation allowance release); pretax margin is about 9.1% [2][7]. Forward P/E is derived from the $24.15 price and FY2027 consensus EPS of $1.07. Daily dollar volume is about $80M, well above the liquidity floor [4].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (6/9): Cross-border remittances require money-transmitter licenses, AML/KYC compliance and payout partnerships across nearly 150 countries, which AI cannot replicate. Motley Fool/Nasdaq analysis notes there are no signs Remitly is being disrupted by AI and calls it more insulated than many fintech peers [10]. The more credible technology threat is stablecoin and real-time payment rails compressing take rates, flagged in a March 2025 short-seller report. The gap between 27% send-volume growth and 20% revenue growth suggests pricing pressure is already building [7]. AI Opportunity (0/1): AI is used internally for product velocity and customer support, but Remitly reports no AI-attributable revenue [9].

infinite_game.summary: Remitly has a genuine, immigrant-centered cause sustained over 15 years by its founder, and it invested through a decade of losses to build a global licensed network. The founder-to-operator CEO handoff, persistent insider selling and a newer focus on take rate and profitability raise Sinek's question of whether the cause will keep steering decisions as the company matures.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): The purpose, transforming the lives of immigrants and their families, is service-oriented and idealistic, and Oppenheimer's 15-year journey from a mall booth shows it has shaped strategy since founding [12][14]. It has not yet been tested by a leadership transition; Gunningham took over only recently [8].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Glassdoor reviews are mixed. 2026 reviewers describe strong, collaborative colleagues and meaningful work, while a 2024 reviewer called the environment toxic and said leaders did not live the values [11]. The CEO transition adds organizational uncertainty, so trust is adequate but not exceptional [8].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No management commentary was found framing Western Union, Wise or stablecoin-based entrants as rivals that sharpen Remitly's own offering. Public messaging centers on share gains and send-volume growth rather than learning from competitors [6][7].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Remitly moved from a single remittance app toward higher-value senders and broader financial services for immigrants, and it is adopting AI across product development [6][9]. These are incremental extensions; the company has not yet faced a forced reinvention, though stablecoin rails could demand one [7].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Leadership ran the business at heavy losses for years ($118M in FY2023), funding licensing and network buildout before turning profitable in FY2025, a classic long-horizon bet [3]. The founder stepping aside for an operator was itself a deliberate succession choice [8]. Current guidance is driven by profitability and take rate, so a pattern of costly principled decisions is not established.

investment_thesis: Remitly is a high-growth, now-profitable leader in digital remittances. Q2 2026 revenue rose 20% to $495M on 27% send-volume growth, FY2026 guidance has been raised four straight times to $1.978-1.988B (+21-22%), and the balance sheet carries essentially no debt (D/E of 3.4%) [1][6]. At $24.15 the stock trades at about 22.6x FY2027 consensus EPS of $1.07 and roughly 11.7x TTM free cash flow, with analysts modeling EPS rising to $2.13 by FY2029 [3][4]. A licensed network across nearly 150 countries and a mission-led brand among immigrant customers give it a durable position that AI does not threaten [10].
thesis_continued: Revenue is growing about 7 points slower than send volume, a sign of take-rate compression as competition from Wise, legacy players and stablecoin-based rails intensifies [7]. Reported profitability flatters the trend: Q2 2026 net income of $206M included a $141M tax benefit, and pretax margin is only about 9% [2]. Leadership is in transition from founder Matt Oppenheimer to Sebastian Gunningham, insiders have been consistent net sellers with no open-market purchases, and immigration and remittance-tax policy remain exogenous risks to the core customer base [5][8]. Q3 results on November 4, 2026 are a near-term volatility event.
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results on November 4, 2026 against guidance of $505-507M revenue (+20-21%); a fifth consecutive guidance raise would reinforce the compounding story
Continued mix shift to high-value senders and broader immigrant financial products lifting revenue per customer
Operating leverage on a nearly debt-free balance sheet, with consensus EPS climbing from $1.07 (FY2027) to $2.13 (FY2029)
key_risks: Take-rate compression: send volume +27% versus revenue +20% in Q2 2026 as stablecoin and real-time payment rails lower cross-border transfer pricing
US immigration enforcement or remittance excise taxes shrinking the core sender base or raising costs per transaction
Execution risk under a new non-founder CEO, combined with heavy insider selling and earnings quality distorted by a one-time $141M tax benefit
